overview: Imagine a royal message cut into stone in 1135: “Panjalu is victorious.” Beyond it lie Brantas River rice fields, brick sanctuaries, markets, scribes, poets and a court at Daha. This is the historical Kediri kingdom, also called Panjalu. It grew from Airlangga's divided realm around 1042 and lasted until Kertajaya was defeated by Ken Angrok in 1222. Under Jayabhaya, poets completed the Bhāratayuddha, remaking an Indian epic in Old Javanese rather than merely copying it. Farmers and water managers inherited dams and channels built to tame the flood-prone Brantas. Traders connected Java to sea routes, while inscriptions recorded tax privileges, officials, craftspeople and healers. Yet evidence is lopsided: stone orders and court poems survive better than children's lessons, wooden homes or toilets. The atlas creates a second puzzle. Its exact “Kediri” layer begins in 1279, fifty-seven years after the kingdom ended, continues through the Majapahit age to 1492, and stretches from Java into southern Borneo and eastern Sumbawa. That is not historical Kediri. This card tells the historical story while marking the imported dates and shape as a serious data error.

periods.title: A divided Airlangga realm
periods.summary: Airlangga retired around 1042 after arranging a division commonly remembered as Janggala and Panjalu. The exact boundary and the earliest succession remain debated, so this is a cautious opening rather than a sharp founding day.

periods.title: Panjalu emerges through a thin record
periods.summary: Later traditions and scattered inscriptions point toward Panjalu or Kediri becoming the stronger western kingdom, but the sequence is incomplete. Blank years in the inscription record must not be filled with invented rulers or borders.

periods.title: Bameswara in dated inscriptions
periods.summary: Padlĕgan I names Bameswara in 1117, and the 1120 Panumbangan order records a royal sima grant. These documents make administration visible while revealing only selected transactions, not a complete kingdom census.

periods.title: Jayabhaya and victorious Panjalu
periods.summary: Jayabhaya issued the Hantang inscription in 1135 with the phrase pañjalu jayati. His court later sponsored the Bhāratayuddha, completed in 1157, joining political confidence to extraordinary Old Javanese literary work.

periods.title: Successors known unevenly
periods.summary: Dated inscriptions name rulers after Jayabhaya, including Sarweswara and Aryyeswara, but evidence does not support a smooth modern-style reign chart. The court and local institutions continued through gaps in what survives.

periods.title: Kameswara and court poetry
periods.summary: Kameswara is associated with the late twelfth-century court and works such as Smaradahana. Surviving manuscripts are later copies, so composition, patronage and the physical page now read are three different dates.

periods.title: Śrṅga, Kĕmulan and Palah
periods.summary: Kĕmulan evidence dates to 1194, while the 1197 Palah inscription invokes King Śrṅga. That early sacred foundation must be separated from the large Panataran monuments mainly built under later Majapahit rulers.

periods.title: Kertajaya and the 1222 defeat
periods.summary: Textual traditions call the last ruler Kertajaya or Śrṅga. Ken Angrok defeated him in 1222, transferring political power toward Singhasari. The people, fields, stories and sacred places did not vanish with one royal defeat.

items.text: The exact indexed record is id “kediri,” label “Kediri,” circa 1279 to 1492, generated from historical basemaps. It has three border intervals and had no card or override at audit time. Its own imported summary describes the older Panjalu kingdom, exposing a date-content contradiction inside the dataset.

Historical Kediri or Panjalu belongs roughly to the mid-eleventh century through 1222. The atlas starts its feature in 1279, fifty-seven years after Ken Angrok defeated Kertajaya, and continues it through the Majapahit age. The displayed interval therefore cannot be used as the kingdom's historical lifespan.

The 1279 feature is a MultiPolygon with four parts, four rings and 152 positions. Its bounds are 109.115° to 118.983° east and 9.177° south to 1.369° south. Its coordinate SHA-256 is f83aa5c5eb3c6adf43527c2983265bfb6144715d713e14afd20eb7f9db0c1753. Those numbers audit a display object, not royal control.

Point tests place Daha, Kelud, Trowulan, Singhasari, Yogyakarta and Semarang inside, but also Banjarmasin in southern Borneo and Bima in eastern Sumbawa. Meanwhile the Brantas delta, Janggala or Sidoarjo, Surabaya and Tuban fall outside. This is far too broad and strangely selective for historical Panjalu.

The 1300 geometry is byte-for-byte identical to 1279. At 1400 it keeps four parts and 152 positions with only tiny coordinate changes, producing SHA-256 17651100a0500fdc3fe8dcd9fb6a7b1819d9311c21f42695b3dbcf85fd429642. The same footprint persisted for more than a century. Repetition across seams makes the error durable; it does not make it historical.

At 1200, during the real Kediri period, the atlas uses the generic id “east-java” with almost the same giant geometry. That feature cannot be silently renamed Kediri because East Java also contained Janggala and, after 1222, Singhasari. A regional bucket is not a tested political alias.

Singhasari begins with Ken Angrok's victory in 1222 and belongs to much of the century that the atlas assigns to “east-java” and then “kediri.” No exact singhasari id exists in the imported index. Its absence is a catalog problem, not evidence that Kediri survived under another label.

Majapahit began in 1293 and has a separate coverage record and card even though it lacks an imported border feature. The atlas “kediri” polygon overlaps Majapahit's entire era. It must never become an alias for Majapahit merely because the broad shape resembles later Javanese power.

Daha or Kediri remained an important place-name after 1222, and later rulers could claim Kediri connections. Those later political identities, including fifteenth-century Daha or Girindrawardhana contexts, are not automatically the eleventh- to thirteenth-century Panjalu kingdom. A familiar place can outlive several states.

At 1492 the exact target vanishes and the atlas assigns all tested Java, Borneo and Bima points to “malaysian-islamic-states.” That seam is historically impossible and supplies no conqueror. The override therefore records no fall or successor, while the card gives the actual Kediri ending in 1222.

sections.title: Follow rulers, conflict and diplomacy carefully

items.text: Airlangga's 1041 Pucangan inscription and his retirement around 1042 anchor the background. Tradition describes a split between Janggala and Panjalu, perhaps to manage succession. The names are useful, but historians debate the exact mechanics and borders, so no ruler drew the atlas shape shown here.

Bameswara appears in dated Kediri inscriptions from 1117. A 1120 order connected with Panumbangan granted sima status, meaning specified fiscal privileges and duties. It shows a king rewarding or reorganizing a locality through a formal document, not abolishing every other levy across the realm.

Jayabhaya's 1135 Hantang inscription celebrates Panjalu victory. The enemy and full campaign are harder to reconstruct than the slogan, so the card does not manufacture a battle map. A victory formula proves royal commemoration; it cannot tell us how many fought or what every village experienced.

Inscriptions name a succession of rulers after Jayabhaya, but their reign boundaries are not a continuous official calendar. Archaeological surveys use dated charters and regnal titles to build a sequence while leaving gaps visible. Uncertainty is evidence about survival, not permission to invent palace drama.

Sources remember Kertajaya, also connected with the name Śrṅga, in conflict with Ken Angrok. The decisive defeat came in 1222 and shifted the political center toward Singhasari. Later chronicles add memorable scenes; historians compare them with inscriptions instead of treating every episode as eyewitness reporting.

Royal inscriptions were official acts, commonly cut on stone or copper and sometimes known on palm leaf. They could establish privileges, obligations, boundaries, witnesses and curses. Because rulers chose what deserved durable recording, inscriptions illuminate administration while favoring exceptional grants over ordinary days.

Sima land was relieved from specified burdens and assigned duties, often supporting a sanctuary or rewarding service. Charters list royal officials, gifts, taxes, witnesses and oath ceremonies. “Tax-free” is too simple: residents might exchange one set of payments for another lasting obligation.

Specialist citralekha prepared inscriptions. They needed command of Old Javanese language and script, royal formulae and bureaucratic order. Their work joins education to government: a crooked letter was not merely untidy when it helped define land, dues and a king's command.

Chinese reports describe ministers, hundreds of lower officials, treasuries and granaries in “Java.” This can suggest organized court government near the Kediri era, but the report compresses information from different times and places. It should corroborate broad capacity, not supply a precise Kediri civil-service chart.

The title taṇḍa appears for elite guards or warriors in Old Javanese literary and epigraphic records from Kediri onward. Comparing poem and inscription helps identify a real office without assuming every flamboyant literary duel happened exactly as sung. Court security, military status and storytelling overlapped but were not identical.

sections.title: Work with the Brantas and wider trade

items.text: Kediri's heartland lay along the Brantas basin near Daha. Rice farming benefited from fertile volcanic soils but also faced Kelud eruptions and a river that could flood or change course. Geography offered food and movement only when communities maintained fields, banks, crossings and channels.

In 1037, just before the partition, Airlangga's government and local communities built the Wringin Sapta dam to control Brantas flooding that disrupted fields and boats. Kediri inherited this engineered landscape. The dam is close background, not an invention that should be credited to Jayabhaya.

Old Javanese inscriptions use terms for dams, dikes, reservoirs, tunnels and channels, and name water-related officials. Such systems required repeated clearing and repair; one royal inauguration could not stop mud, roots or monsoon damage forever. Irrigation was organized labor as much as a clever structure.

A Chinese compilation near the end of the Kediri age describes Java growing rice, millet, beans, sugarcane, bananas and taro, ploughing with buffaloes and collecting a rice-related rent. It is regional outsider evidence, not a menu or tax receipt from every village around Daha.

The same account lists foreign merchants, metals, silks, ceramics, aromatics and pepper exchange. River routes connected interior production with ports, but the atlas strangely excludes much of the Brantas delta. Trade goods reveal networks; they do not prove Panjalu ruled every place where a jar or coin traveled.

The Bhāratayuddha was completed in 1157 by Mpu Sedah and Mpu Panuluh under Jayabhaya's patronage. It retold the Mahābhārata war in Old Javanese kakawin form. Adaptation required mastery of language, meter and court culture; this was creative scholarship, not ancient copy-and-paste.

Other kakawin associated with Kediri courts include Hariwangsa, Ghaṭotkacāśraya and Smaradahana. Patron and date assignments differ in confidence. Lists of titles show a lively literary world, but they cannot tell how many listeners understood every Sanskrit allusion or owned a manuscript.

The 1157 composition survives through later manuscript traditions, especially in Bali. A copied palm-leaf page may be centuries younger than the poem it carries, and scribes could adapt wording. Historians separate original court context, later recopying and modern printed edition instead of assigning one date to all three.

Śaiva, Buddhist and other Indic traditions appear in texts, inscriptions and sculpture. Tondowongso finds include Brahma, Candra, Surya, Nandi and a yoni. That group illuminates a sacred complex; it does not prove every Kediri subject followed one identical ritual practice.

Learning likely happened through court and religious specialists, scribal apprenticeship, memorization and household practice. The technical skill of poets and citralekha is secure; an ordinary-child school schedule is not. The evidence supports trained learners without supplying enrollment rates, classrooms or universal literacy.

Tondowongso preserves a brick sanctuary complex with sculpture and an eleventh- to thirteenth-century horizon. Excavation connects it to the broad Airlangga-Kediri age, yet dating individual construction phases remains difficult. A religious compound is excellent craft evidence and a poor blueprint for an ordinary home.

At Besole, archaeologists studied brick remains and a gateway in a landscape connected with Kediri-period inscriptions. Attribution is cautious because buildings can be repaired, reused or rebuilt. A brick that sits in Kediri country is not automatically stamped with one ruler's name.

The Palah inscription of 1197 records devotion under King Śrṅga at the place later called Panataran. Most impressive monuments visible in the surviving complex belong to Majapahit centuries, however. The early inscription proves sacred continuity, not that Kertajaya commissioned every tower tourists see.

Brahma, Candra, Surya, Nandi and yoni finds show quarrying, stone selection, iconographic planning and skilled carving. Some objects were unfinished or displaced, and research continues. Archaeologists compare style, material and context rather than sorting every statue by the nearest famous king.

Very little stone sculpture can be assigned securely to Kediri. The huge Boro Gaṇeśa is debated around the Kediri-Singhasari transition, and its carved textile patterns invite comparison with traded cloth. The honest achievement story includes masterpieces, disputed dates and a large missing record.

sections.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children

items.text: Court poems describe marriages, longing, kin and ceremony, but their heroes are not a census. Research across Old Javanese kakawin finds arranged marriage, elopement or abduction themes and cousin marriage, while warning that one later poem cannot simply be backdated into every Kediri household.

Society included royal families, high officials, religious specialists, guards, scribes, village authorities, farmers, traders, artisans, performers and dependent laborers. Rank shaped obligations and rewards. Inscriptions reveal named categories better than personal feelings, so a tax list cannot explain how every family negotiated status.

Women appear in literary marriage stories and in the work of textile production, exchange and household life, but direct Kediri biographies are rare. Elite heroines cannot stand for all women, and silence in a royal inscription does not mean women were absent from farms, markets or ritual.

Children probably learned by watching work, memorizing stories and prayers, practicing crafts or letters when their household had access. Specialist poets and inscription writers prove advanced teaching existed. No consulted source provides a typical Kediri child's timetable, school age or literacy percentage, so none is invented.

Kakawin were made for skilled performance and listening as well as reading. Music, recitation and dramatic movement could carry stories beyond the small group able to write difficult meters. Even so, audience size and access varied; “court culture” should not be stretched into universal entertainment.

sections.title: Eat, dress, live, work and play

items.text: Near-contemporary Chinese reporting lists rice, millet, beans, gourds, coconut, banana, sugarcane, taro, fish, fowl, ducks and goats for Java. It also mentions salt boiled from seawater. This is a regional abundance list, not proof that every inland child ate meat, sugar or imported spice daily.

Textiles moved as valuable goods, payments and signs of status. Old Javanese writing names cloth in gifts and ceremony, while sculpture preserves carved patterns. Fiber, weave and decoration depended on wealth and setting; a jeweled court garment would have been wildly impractical in a muddy rice field.

Wood, bamboo, thatch and earth likely made many homes, which helps explain why temples and inscriptions dominate archaeology. A Chinese account praises painted dwellings and merchant lodges, but it describes “Java” through outsider reports. No secure standard Kediri house plan survives to furnish room by room.

Work joined farmers and buffalo teams, water managers, boat crews, traders, builders, stone carvers, textile makers, performers, guards and scribes. Inscriptions name specialized service categories, but occupation could overlap with household and seasonal labor. One title does not freeze a person into a modern job description.

A Chinese report mentions boat outings, hill trips, flutes, drums, castanets, mime, cockfighting and pig fighting in Java. These vivid details may reflect elite spectacle, regional custom or recycled information. They are evidence for reported amusements, not permission to schedule every Kediri child for a pig match.

sections.title: Test medicine, sanitation, writing and continuity

items.text: The 1194 Kĕmulan inscription includes walyan, interpreted as a healer, among named specialists. That direct local term is strong evidence that healers existed, but the charter names a category rather than a remedy. It reveals neither treatment recipes, success rates nor access for an ordinary family.

Brantas dams, channels and reservoirs supported fields, transport and flood control. Sacred water structures served ritual purposes. None of those automatically supplied safe drinking water: irrigation, bathing and household water are different systems, and consulted Kediri sources do not describe routine boiling, wells or water quality.

No consulted authoritative source securely identifies an ordinary Kediri household toilet, sewer network, garbage collection schedule or handwashing rule. Organic structures rarely survive, and temple drains are not toilets. The safest reconstruction is an explicit gap, not a suspiciously modern bathroom built from silence.

Authentic sample, 1135 CE Hantang inscription, National Museum D 9: scholarly transliteration “pañjalu jayati”; translation, “Panjalu is victorious.” It is a short Sanskrit victory formula inside an Old Javanese inscription cut in Kediri quadrate script. Original glyphs are not reproduced because Unicode text would not be a facsimile of the carved forms.

The kingdom ended politically with Kertajaya's defeat in 1222, but Daha, fields, temples, language and stories continued under new rulers. Panji tales later spread through many regions and versions. That cultural afterlife is continuity, not proof that the same Kediri state ruled until the atlas endpoint of 1492.

ending.text: Ken Angrok defeated Kertajaya in 1222, ending Kediri or Panjalu as the dominant independent kingdom and opening Singhasari rule. The successor has no exact imported id, so no invented link is added. Daha and its communities remained important, Old Javanese works continued through later copies and adaptation, and Panji traditions traveled far beyond East Java. The atlas feature's 1279 start and 1492 disappearance are data seams, not the kingdom's birth and fall.
